source: GG14 ch5, ch9, ch46; GG12 ch39, ch41; RangDale9 ch19, ch59; KDT8 ch3

cards.front: How are immunoassays for hCG used?
cards.back: Home pregnancy kits use antibodies specific for the unique beta subunit of hCG to detect pregnancy qualitatively within a few days of a missed period. Quantitative plasma hCG by radioimmunoassay shows whether pregnancy is progressing normally, helps detect ectopic pregnancy, hydatidiform mole and choriocarcinoma, and follows hCG-secreting germ cell tumours.

cards.front: How did monoclonal antibodies help quantitative peptide pharmacology?
cards.back: They made radioimmunoassay and immunocytochemistry of peptides possible, solving many measurement problems; sensitive assays for mRNA and in situ hybridisation also map precursor synthesis.

cards.front: What is the principle of ELISA?
cards.back: Antigen-antibody binding gives specificity. A labelled enzyme produces a coloured or fluorescent product from a substrate, and the signal read by a plate reader is proportional to the amount of antigen or antibody, giving sensitivity.

cards.front: What are the five steps of a general ELISA?
cards.back: Coat the microtitre wells with antigen. Block unbound sites to prevent false positives. Add the primary antibody. Add an enzyme-linked secondary antibody. Add the substrate, which forms a coloured product. With HRP and TMB, acid turns the colour yellow, which is read at 450 nm.

cards.front: Give clinical uses of ELISA kits for gonadotropins.
cards.back: Over-the-counter urinary LH ELISA kits detect the LH surge (tested every 12-24 h from about day 10-12 of a 28-day cycle) to predict ovulation, which occurs about 36 h after the surge begins. Beta-subunit-specific ELISA of plasma LH and FSH helps localise reproductive disease: low levels point to hypothalamic or pituitary disease, high levels to primary gonadal failure; raised FSH also confirms menopause.

cards.front: Which immunoassays are used for thyroid function tests, and what is the gold standard for free T4?
cards.back: Radioimmunoassays and, more recently, chemiluminescent and enzyme-linked immunoassays for T4, T3 and TSH; routine free T4 and T3 assays use labelled hormone analogues. The gold standard for free T4 is equilibrium dialysis of undiluted serum followed by radioimmunoassay of the dialysate, which is rarely available routinely.

cards.front: Short note: Types of ELISA

points: Labelled primary antibody binds antigen on the plate
Fastest, fewest steps
Lower sensitivity; each primary antibody must be labelled
Unlabelled primary antibody, then labelled secondary antibody
High sensitivity; one secondary serves many primary antibodies
Risk of cross-reaction by the secondary antibody
Capture antibody on the plate, then antigen, then detection antibody
Highly sensitive for antigen detection
Sample antigen competes with labelled antigen for antibody sites
Higher sample antigen gives a weaker signal
Works with crude or impure samples

cards.front: How does fluorescence polarization immunoassay (FPIA) measure a drug in serum?
cards.back: A fluorescein-labelled drug competes with the patient's own drug for a limited number of antibody sites. Bound tracer tumbles slowly and emits more polarised light. More drug in the sample means less labelled drug bound and a lower reading. Used for drugs of abuse such as amphetamines, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, cocaine and opiates.

cards.front: Why has radioimmunoassay largely been replaced by ELISA?
cards.back: RIA uses antigens labelled with radioisotopes. It is highly sensitive and specific, but the radioisotopes need special safety measures. ELISA replaces the radioisotope with an enzyme, so RIA is now rarely used in clinical laboratories.

cards.front: List the advantages and disadvantages of radioimmunoassay.
cards.back: Advantages: very sensitive (picogram amounts with high-affinity antibody), highly specific, used for hormones and for drugs such as digoxin and some drugs of abuse. Disadvantages: radiolabel is costly and short-lived, gamma emission needs special counters, radioactive iodine concentrates in the thyroid if taken in accidentally, needs licence, disposal and trained staff, narrow assay range, hard to automate. Hence ELISA, which uses an enzyme label, has largely replaced it.

cards.front: Short note: Radioimmunoassay (principle)

points: Physico-chemical test-tube assay based on antigen-antibody binding, not a bioassay in animals or tissue
Measures hormones and drugs in plasma
Radioiodine-labelled hormone (or drug)
Specific antibody, usually from immunised animal serum (polyclonal); monoclonal antibodies give superior assays
Unlabelled standard and the unknown sample
Labelled and unlabelled hormone compete for the same antibody
Bound (B) to free (F) labelled hormone ratio falls as unlabelled hormone rises
Standard curve: B/F ratio plotted against known standard concentrations
Unknown plasma run under the same conditions; concentration read off the curve
Detects minute quantities of circulating hormones and other active substances

cards.front: Essay: Immunoassays used in pharmacology (RIA, ELISA, FPIA)

points: Specific antigen-antibody binding measures hormones, drugs and toxins in small samples
Radiolabelled antigen competes with sample antigen for limited antibody sites; bound/free ratio falls as sample antigen rises
Very sensitive but radiation hazard, cost and short isotope life
Enzyme label gives a coloured or fluorescent product read by a plate reader; direct, indirect, sandwich and competitive formats
Replaces the radioisotope, so now preferred
Fluorescein-labelled drug competes with patient drug for antibody; more drug in the sample gives less polarised light
Homogeneous and fast; used for drug levels and drugs of abuse
Gonadotropin and hCG tests, thyroid tests, digoxin levels, urine drug screens

cards.front: State the Beer-Lambert law as applied in spectrophotometry.
cards.back: Absorbance equals the molar absorption coefficient times the molar concentration times the path length of the solution. At a fixed wavelength, absorbance is directly proportional to concentration, so an unknown concentration is found from its absorbance.

cards.front: What are the uses of UV-visible spectrophotometry?
cards.back: Measuring concentration, identifying compounds by their absorption maximum (lambda max), colour determination in the 380-700 nm range, quantifying DNA, RNA and proteins, and following reaction kinetics.

cards.front: What is the principle of colorimetry?
cards.back: Colour development is linked to the concentration of a substance in solution. The concentration can therefore be measured from the extent of light absorption at the appropriate wavelength.

cards.front: What happens to the sample in the flame in flame photometry?
cards.back: The solution evaporates and the substance becomes free atoms. Their electrons are lifted to a higher energy state, then fall back and release the energy as light.

cards.front: Why can each metal be identified in flame photometry?
cards.back: The wavelength of light emitted depends on the energy levels the electrons can reach, which are specific to each element (its emission spectrum). So the emitted colour identifies the metal.

cards.front: Which clinical analyte does flame photometry measure routinely?
cards.back: Sodium and potassium in body fluids such as blood serum.

cards.front: How is the concentration of a metal found in flame photometry?
cards.back: Light emitted is collected by a reflector and falls on a detector, and detector output is directly proportional to concentration. So solutions of known strength (standards) are read first, and the unknown sample reading is compared with them.

cards.front: Why does haemoglobin look red, and how does the Beer-Lambert law let you measure it?
cards.back: Haemoglobin absorbs blue and green light much more than red, so red light is what reaches the eye. The more haemoglobin in the cuvette, the more blue-green light is absorbed, and at a fixed wavelength absorbance rises in direct proportion to concentration (Beer-Lambert). So the photometer reading of the absorbed light gives the concentration.

cards.front: In colorimetry, why is a colour filter used, and how is an unknown concentration found?
cards.back: The filter has the colour complementary to the absorbing substance so it selects the wavelength the substance absorbs; colorimetry works only in the visible range. The photocell reading is zeroed with solvent, then absorbance of standards is plotted against concentration, and the test solution's absorbance is read off this calibration curve.

cards.front: Short note: UV-visible spectrophotometry

points: Light source: tungsten, hydrogen or deuterium lamp, or xenon flash lamp
Monochromator (entrance slit, exit slit, dispersion device) gives one wavelength
Cuvette of plastic, glass or optical-grade quartz, in a darkened chamber
Photodetector converts light intensity to current; read on a meter, LCD or computer
Concentration of a solution, and quantification of DNA, RNA and proteins
Identify organic compounds by the absorption maximum (lambda max)
Colour determination in the 380-700 nm range
Detect impurities, follow reaction kinetics, measure enzyme activity and protein concentration

cards.front: Short note: Flame photometer components

points: Relatively low-energy flame excites only a few elements, mainly alkali metals
Reflector collects the light emitted in all directions and passes it to the detector
Detector output is directly proportional to concentration
Standards of known strength are read first, then the unknown sample

cards.front: What role did HPLC play in peptide pharmacology?
cards.back: From the 1970s, techniques to purify, sequence and synthesise peptides were developed; high-performance liquid chromatography together with solid-phase peptide synthesis greatly accelerated the field.

cards.front: Which analytical platforms underlie metabolomics in drug development?
cards.back: Proton NMR and liquid or gas chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry, with chemometric and multivariate analysis. They measure thousands of chemicals in serum, urine, cells or tissue at once and can screen for drug toxicity in whole animals during preclinical development.

cards.front: What is HPLC and how does it differ from column chromatography?
cards.back: A separation technique in which solvent is forced through a column under high pressure (up to about 400 atmospheres) instead of dripping under gravity, so separation is much faster and uses much smaller particles. Components are identified by retention time and quantified from peak area.

cards.front: What is thin-layer chromatography used for?
cards.back: It is a planar chromatography technique that separates the components of a mixture, such as alkaloids or phospholipids. It is cheap and quick for qualitative checks of purity, and only semi-quantitative.

cards.front: What is the retention factor (Rf) in thin-layer chromatography?
cards.back: Distance travelled by a compound divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front. It is a fixed value for a compound under set conditions, so it helps identify spots.

cards.front: What are retention time and peak area in HPLC, and what does each tell you?
cards.back: Retention time is the time from injection to the peak maximum for a compound; it helps identify the compound, provided pressure, stationary phase, solvent mix and column temperature are held constant. Area under the peak is proportional to the amount passing the detector, so it measures quantity; a more dilute sample gives a smaller area but the same retention time.

cards.front: What is mass spectrometry and what are its three main parts?
cards.back: It identifies and quantifies chemicals by turning them into gas-phase ions and sorting the ions by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) and abundance, giving a spectrum of abundance against m/z. Parts: ion source (makes ions), analyser (separates by m/z), detector (records abundance of each ion).

cards.front: How is HPLC used for detection, and what is reversed-phase HPLC?
cards.back: A UV detector after the column measures absorbance of eluting compounds, giving peaks. Reversed-phase HPLC, the most common form, uses a nonpolar hydrocarbon-bonded silica column with a polar solvent such as water and methanol. Coupling to mass spectrometry adds identification from fragmentation patterns.

cards.front: Contrast normal-phase and reversed-phase HPLC. Which elutes polar compounds first, and which is more common?
cards.back: Normal phase: polar silica column with a non-polar solvent such as hexane, so polar compounds stick longer and non-polar ones emerge first. Reversed phase: silica made non-polar with long hydrocarbon chains and a polar solvent such as water-methanol, so polar compounds travel with the solvent and emerge first. Reversed phase is the commonest form.

cards.front: Why is a chromatograph coupled to a mass spectrometer (GC-MS, LC-MS)?
cards.back: The chromatograph separates the mixture and the mass spectrometer then fragments each fraction into a pattern that can be matched against a database. Compounds can be identified without knowing their retention times, and drugs or metabolites in biological samples can be quantified. This is why GC-MS and LC-MS are used for forensic drug confirmation and metabolomics.

cards.front: Short note: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)

points: Improved column chromatography: solvent forced through the column at very high pressure (up to about 400 atmospheres)
Very small packing particles give a large surface area and better separation; detection is automated and sensitive
Normal phase: polar silica, non-polar solvent
Reversed phase: non-polar bonded silica, polar solvent; the commonest form
UV detector after the column gives peaks
Retention time identifies a compound; peak area measures its amount
Can be coupled to a mass spectrometer for fragmentation-based identification
Drug and metabolite quantification in biological samples, forensic testing (e.g. anabolic steroids, benzodiazepines)
Pharmaceutical quality control, shelf-life and dissolution studies

cards.front: Short note: Mass spectrometry in pharmacology

Plot of ion abundance against m/z identifies and quantifies the molecule
Electron impact, chemical ionisation, fast atom bombardment, field ionisation, plasma desorption
GC-MS, LC-MS, HPLC-MS: chromatograph separates, MS identifies
Metabolomics, forensic confirmation of drug abuse, drug monitoring
Drug discovery, early phase ADME studies and metabolite screening

cards.front: How was potassium measured in the Langendorff heart method for cardiac glycosides?
cards.back: By flame photometry of the coronary outflow. An increase in potassium outflow correlated well with the positive inotropic effect of the glycoside.

cards.front: Why do drug levels need to be measured at all when a standard dose is given?
cards.back: The steady-state level actually reached can be anywhere from about one third to three times the value predicted from population averages, because patients differ in absorption, clearance and other factors. A measured level lets the dose rate be corrected in proportion to the target level.

cards.front: Drugs for which therapeutic drug monitoring is useful
cards.text: Therapeutic drug monitoring helps for drugs with a low safety margin such as {{digoxin}}, {{anticonvulsants}}, {{antiarrhythmics}}, {{theophylline}}, {{aminoglycosides}}, {{lithium}} and {{tricyclic antidepressants}}.

cards.front: List the situations in which measuring plasma drug levels is particularly useful.
cards.back: Low safety margin; wide individual variation in kinetics; a toxic drug in a patient with renal failure; suspected poisoning; unexplained treatment failure; and checking patient compliance (a random level is enough for this). The common thread is that the dose alone cannot be trusted to give a safe, effective level.

cards.front: What are the uses and pitfalls of urine toxicology immunoassay screens?
cards.back: They rapidly (about 1 h) detect common drugs of abuse: amphetamines, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, cannabis, cocaine and opiates. Results must be read with caution: cross-reactivity gives false positives and long detection windows may not reflect acute toxicity, so further tests should be tailored to the case.

cards.front: Which analytical methods identify toxins qualitatively, and which quantify them?
cards.back: Colorimetric and UV-visible spectrophotometric analysis can be used for qualitative analysis of toxins. Infrared spectroscopy, gas chromatography, HPLC and immunoassay are used to quantify toxins.

cards.front: When in the dosing interval should a sample be drawn for TDM, and why does it differ between drugs?
cards.back: For long-acting or continuously acting drugs, take a trough steady-state sample just before the next dose, since levels barely fluctuate and trough guards against accumulation or under-dosing. For short-acting drugs given intermittently (e.g. ampicillin, gentamicin), sample in the post-absorptive phase about 1-2 h after an oral or i.m. dose to reflect the peak. In poisoning, sample as early as possible and repeat to estimate clearance and the need to hasten elimination, e.g. by haemodialysis.

cards.front: Why is plasma level monitoring of no value for some drugs? Give examples for each reason.
cards.back: Level monitoring only helps when plasma concentration tracks effect. Easily measured response: antihypertensives, hypoglycaemics, diuretics, oral anticoagulants, inhalational anaesthetics. Drug activated in the body: levodopa. Hit-and-run drugs whose effect outlasts the plasma level: reserpine, guanethidine, MAO inhibitors, omeprazole. Irreversible binding: organophosphates, phenoxybenzamine.

cards.front: Short note: Therapeutic drug monitoring (application of drug estimation)

points: Steady-state level may be 1/3 to 3 times the predicted value
Measured level allows dose correction: revised dose rate = previous rate x target/measured Css (first-order drugs)
Low safety margin: digoxin, anticonvulsants, antiarrhythmics, theophylline, aminoglycosides, lithium, tricyclics
Large individual variation
Toxic drugs in renal failure (aminoglycosides, vancomycin)
Poisoning; unexplained failure; checking compliance
Trough for continuously acting drugs
Peak 1-2 h after dose for intermittently acting drugs (ampicillin, gentamicin)
Early and repeated samples in poisoning
Easily measured response (antihypertensives, hypoglycaemics)
Prodrugs (levodopa); hit-and-run drugs; irreversible drugs

cards.front: Essay: Therapeutic drug monitoring - principles, methods, advantages and limitations

points: Using measured drug levels to individualise dose; steady-state level may be 1/3 to 3 times the predicted value

Immunoassays (RIA, FPIA, ELISA) and chromatography with mass spectrometry for drug and toxin levels

cards.front: Which analytical techniques are used for drug testing in sport?
cards.back: Blood or urine samples are analysed under strict protocols in approved laboratories, mainly by gas chromatography/mass spectrometry or immunoassay.

cards.front: What is the T/E ratio and why does it rise after exogenous testosterone?
cards.back: T/E is urinary testosterone glucuronide divided by epitestosterone glucuronide, its endogenous epimer. Giving testosterone suppresses the body's own secretion of both steroids and replaces them with testosterone alone, so the ratio rises above normal.

cards.front: Why is tetrahydrogestrinone (THG) a problem for doping control?
cards.back: It is a potent androgen that appears to have been designed to escape antidoping laboratories, both through its novel structure, so routine tests for known androgens could miss it.

cards.front: When can ordinary gas chromatography-mass spectrometry detect doping with an androgen?
cards.back: It detects androgens other than testosterone itself, but only if the athlete is still taking the drug when tested. Testosterone is handled separately because the body also makes it, so detection needs the T/E ratio or isotope-ratio mass spectrometry.

cards.front: How is misuse of exogenous testosterone detected?
cards.back: Other androgens are found by gas chromatography and mass spectrometry if still being taken. Testosterone itself is detected by a raised urinary testosterone/epitestosterone glucuronide (T/E) ratio, limited by UDP-glucuronosyl transferase polymorphism, or by gas chromatography-combustion-isotope ratio mass spectrometry: a low 13C/12C ratio indicates a pharmaceutical source.

cards.front: How does isotope-ratio mass spectrometry confirm exogenous testosterone, and what does a low 13C/12C ratio mean?
cards.back: Gas chromatography-combustion-isotope ratio mass spectrometry measures 13C/12C in urinary steroids. A low ratio means the steroid probably came from a pharmaceutical source rather than the body. It is the second method for testosterone, used alongside the T/E ratio.

cards.front: Short note: Drug testing in sport (doping control)

points: Blood or urine analysed under strict protocols in approved laboratories
Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry or immunoassay
Androgens other than testosterone: GC-MS if still being taken
Testosterone: raised T/E ratio, and 13C/12C isotope-ratio MS (low ratio means pharmaceutical)
Recombinant erythropoietin: misused for blood doping (epoetin alfa)
Designer androgens such as THG built to evade detection

cards.front: What is the physical half-life of 131I?
cards.back: About 8 days, the physical half-life of 131I, so its activity falls by half in that time.

cards.front: Which emissions of 131I are used for tracing and which for therapy?
cards.back: Gamma rays are used for tracing because a counter can monitor them outside the body. Beta particles are used therapeutically, destroying thyroid cells.

cards.front: Which stable iodine isotope is the non-radioactive form, and how does 131I behave chemically?
cards.back: 127I is stable. 131I behaves chemically like the stable isotope, so the thyroid handles it in the same way.

cards.front: Short note: Radioactive iodine (131I) therapy

points: Sodium salt of 131I given orally in water; concentrated by the thyroid and held in the colloid
Beta emission destroys thyroid tissue from within; neighbouring tissue is spared at chosen doses
Commonest indication is hyperthyroidism
Diagnostic dose (25-100 microcurie) is counted or scanned at intervals
Simple, outpatient, inexpensive
No surgical risk, scar or parathyroid/recurrent laryngeal injury
Once hyperthyroidism is controlled, cure is permanent
About 20-40% need one or more repeat doses
Thyroid status is checked about 3 months after the dose

cards.front: Essay: Radio-isotopes in pharmacology

points: Radioisotopes are unstable nuclei that emit gamma or beta radiation; their half-life sets how long they stay usable
Example: 131I, physical half-life about 8 days
Radiolabelled ligands isolate and characterise receptors (e.g. labelled alpha-bungarotoxin)
Radioiodine uptake and scan tests thyroid function
Radioimmunoassay (RIA) measures hormones and drugs: radiolabelled and unlabelled antigen compete for limited antibody
Quantitative hCG and digoxin levels by RIA
131I ablates thyroid tissue in hyperthyroidism
131I is favoured for radioimmunoconjugates: readily available, inexpensive and easily linked to a monoclonal antibody
Short half-life limits storage; radiation handling needed

Radioisotopes serve as tracers, diagnostic labels and therapeutic agents in pharmacology

cards.front: What does PCR amplify, and how quickly?
cards.back: A specific target DNA sequence, exponentially, giving millions of copies in a short time.

cards.front: What are the three steps of one PCR cycle?
cards.back: Denaturation of template DNA and primer; annealing of primer to the single strand; extension (elongation) of the new strand.

cards.front: Which enzyme and buffer ions does a PCR run need?
cards.back: DNA polymerase plus a buffer containing the cofactors the enzyme needs, with primers and dNTPs. Extension time depends on the polymerase chosen.

cards.front: How are PCR-amplified DNA fragments separated and seen?
cards.back: Agarose gel electrophoresis, then staining with ethidium bromide, which binds DNA and fluoresces.

cards.front: Short note: Antimicrobial resistance testing

points: Penicillin-binding proteins are the targets of beta-lactams
MRSA carries an acquired PBP with very low affinity for penicillins
MIC and disk diffusion tests show susceptibility in vitro
Lowest concentration that prevents visible growth is the MIC
PCR amplifies a specific DNA target so that it can be identified
16S rRNA primers identify species, e.g. gut bacteria

cards.front: Essay: Polymerase chain reaction: methodology and applications

points: Developed by Kary Mullis in 1984; Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1993

Each cycle: denaturation, annealing of primer, extension by DNA polymerase
Template DNA, primers, DNA polymerase, dNTPs and buffer with enzyme cofactors
Thermal cycling; product checked by agarose gel electrophoresis and ethidium bromide staining
Diagnosis of infectious disease, detected earlier than by serology
Gut microbiome studies: 16S rRNA gene primers; shotgun metagenomics: collect sample, extract DNA, sequence

cards.front: Define the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC).
cards.back: The lowest concentration of an antimicrobial that prevents visible growth of the organism.

cards.front: What is the zone of inhibition in disk diffusion?
cards.back: The clear area around an antibiotic disk on a bacterial lawn where there is no visible growth; it indicates susceptibility.

cards.front: What is biostandardisation?
cards.back: Comparing and adjusting the strength of a sample against a standard under controlled conditions.

cards.front: How is a MIC result used to classify an isolate?
cards.back: The isolate is susceptible if its MIC is at or below the clinical breakpoint for that drug-organism pair.

cards.front: Short note: MIC versus MBC

points: MIC: lowest concentration that stops visible growth
MBC: lowest concentration that kills the organism
A large MBC-to-MIC difference indicates bacteriostatic action
MBC is not used to guide antibiotic selection in practice

cards.front: Essay: Antimicrobial drug assay (in vitro susceptibility and potency)

points: Empirical therapy starts first; definitive identification and susceptibility are usually delayed by 24-48 h
Susceptibility testing guides the definitive choice
Disk diffusion: bacterial lawn plus antibiotic disks; zone of inhibition read after 12-24 h
Dilution (MIC): doubling concentrations, visible growth read after 18-24 h; commercial platforms automate it
Compare the MIC with the consensus breakpoint for the drug-organism pair
MBC-to-MIC ratio separates bactericidal from bacteriostatic action
Bioassay compares the log dose-response curve of the sample with that of a standard (indirect assay)
Microorganisms are among the test systems in bioassays; biostandardisation adjusts strength to the standard
Semisynthetic penicillins are dosed by weight; MIC is given in mcg/mL

In vitro assays link drug activity to clinical choice of antimicrobial

cards.front: Define a biomarker in clinical pharmacology.
cards.back: A characteristic objectively measured as an indicator of normal or pathogenic processes, or of a pharmacological response to treatment.

cards.front: Define a surrogate marker.
cards.back: A biomarker intended to substitute for a clinical endpoint; expected to predict clinical benefit, harm or lack of either.

cards.front: Give an example of a surrogate marker of clinical benefit.
cards.back: Blood pressure: lowering it improves survival in hypertensive patients.

cards.front: Why was reduced ventricular premature depolarisation a misleading surrogate?
cards.back: Flecainide and encainide reduced ventricular premature depolarisations, but the CAST trial showed they increased mortality after myocardial infarction.

cards.front: Name the genetic tests the book cites before prescribing.
cards.back: HLA-B*1502 before carbamazepine (Asian ancestry); G6PD deficiency before rasburicase (African or Mediterranean ancestry); VKORC1 (AA variant) with CYP2C9 to guide initial warfarin dose.

cards.front: Name the two endogenous biomarkers used in transporter drug-drug interaction studies.
cards.back: Coproporphyrin-I for OATP1B-mediated hepatic uptake; N-methylnicotinamide for renal OCT2/MATE transport.

cards.front: Short note: Surrogate endpoint versus clinical endpoint

points: Measures how a patient feels, functions or survives
Ultimate outcome (survival, serious morbidity) or intermediate endpoint with real benefit
A subset of biomarkers that substitutes for a clinical endpoint
Examples in premarketing trials: blood pressure, lipid levels, HbA1c, CD4 count
Flecainide reduced ventricular premature depolarisations yet increased mortality (CAST)
HDL raised but not validated as a surrogate
Needs biological plausibility and validation before a biomarker is accepted as surrogate

cards.front: What is metabolic profiling?
cards.back: Measuring many small-molecule metabolites in a sample at once to fingerprint the body's state, for example toxic injury to liver or kidney.

cards.front: How can metabolic profiling help a new drug candidate before clinical trials?
cards.back: Metabolite fingerprints in animal urine or plasma show organ toxicity, so a toxic candidate can be dropped before expensive human trials.
